title: Rank-two root lists and simple-root interchange seeds
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and let $(G,T=D_A(M),\Phi,\Phi^\vee,\{a,b\},(X_a,X_b))$ be a pinned split realization [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization] of semisimple rank two. Use the canonical root exponentials, linked opposite vectors and representatives $n_a,n_b$ of [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus]. Thus for a root vector $Z\in\mathfrak g_r$, $\exp_r(zZ)$ denotes the associated root-group point, and $\operatorname{Ad}(n)$ is the differential of conjugation by $n$.

After enumerating the simple roots with the short root first when their lengths differ, the positive-root coefficient vectors in the basis $(a,b)$ are exactly one of the following four lists:
$$\begin{array}{c|l}A_1\times A_1&a,b\\ A_2&a,b,c=a+b\\ B_2&a,b,c=a+b,d=2a+b\\ G_2&a,b,c=a+b,d=2a+b,e=3a+b,f=3a+2b.\end{array}$$
In type $A_2$ set $X_c=\operatorname{Ad}(n_b)X_a$. In type $B_2$ set $X_c=\operatorname{Ad}(n_b)X_a$ and $X_d=\operatorname{Ad}(n_a)X_b$. In type $G_2$ set
$$X_c=\operatorname{Ad}(n_b)X_a,\quad X_d=\operatorname{Ad}(n_a)X_c,\quad X_e=-\operatorname{Ad}(n_a)X_b,\quad X_f=\operatorname{Ad}(n_b)X_e.$$
These are generators of their indicated root modules. Put $x_r(z)=\exp_r(zX_r)$, including the given $X_a,X_b$ at the simple roots. The following two tangent identities hold in their specified types:
$$A_2:\ \operatorname{Ad}(n_a)X_b=-X_c,\qquad B_2:\ \operatorname{Ad}(n_a)X_c=-X_c.$$

For each type and each ordered pair $(r,s)$ in the following finite list there are integers $k_{i,j;r,s}$, fixed once for that type, such that the displayed interchange identity holds for every commutative $A$-algebra $R$ and all $x,y\in R$:
$$\begin{array}{c|l} A_2&(a,b)\\ B_2&(a,b),(a,c)\\ G_2&(a,b),(a,c),(a,d),(b,e).\end{array}$$
$$x_s(y)x_r(x)=x_r(x)x_s(y)\prod_{\substack{i,j>0\\ ir+js\in\Phi}}x_{ir+js}(k_{i,j;r,s}x^iy^j).$$
Fix the product order by increasing $(i+j,i)$ in lexicographic order. The integers depend only on the type and this normalization; the assertion is simultaneous for all rings, character lattices and realizations, and is an identity of morphisms, stable under arbitrary base change. No integer is required to be invertible. This assertion concerns just the listed pairs and the two stated tangent identities; it asserts no relation for other root pairs or for words in $n_a,n_b$.

source.place: Section 6.2, Isogeny Theorem Step 2 (rank-two lists and signed root vectors), Step 3, Lemma 6.2.8 and Example 6.2.9, printed pp.205--209; restricted to the listed simple-root pairs. The two isolated signs are the A2 and B2 root-string computations with the displayed normalizations. Read online; local archival copy WANTED. This is an auxiliary formulation by the worker, not a quotation of a source with omitted calculations. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group calculation.

proof.text: Work in $V=\mathbf Q a+\mathbf Q b$. The root-datum axioms give the reflection permutations of the finite spanning root set. Their generated linear group $W$ is finite, since a linear map fixing that set fixes $V$. Average any rational positive definite form over $W$ to obtain an invariant positive definite form $B$. Invariance under $s_r$, together with $s_r(r)=-r$, gives $\langle v,r^\vee\rangle=2B(v,r)/B(r,r)$. Put $u=\langle b,a^\vee\rangle$, $v=\langle a,b^\vee\rangle$. These are integers, have the same sign, and $0\leq uv<4$ by strict positive definiteness on the independent vectors $a,b$. If either were positive, one would be $1$ (their product is $1,2$ or $3$); the corresponding reflection would give the forbidden mixed-sign root $b-a$ or $a-b$. Thus $u=v=0$, or, after ordering the shorter root first, $(u,v)=(-m,-1)$ with $m=1,2,3$. Indeed $u/v=B(b,b)/B(a,a)$ when nonzero.

source.place: Step 2, printed pp.205--206; elementary finite-root-system argument spelling out the four possibilities.

proof.text: Every root is in the orbit of a simple root. To see this without changing the given base, write a positive root $r=ia+jb$ with $i,j\geq0$. If $ij=0$, reducedness gives $r=a$ or $b$. Otherwise $B(r,r)=iB(r,a)+jB(r,b)>0$, so some $\alpha\in\{a,b\}$ has $\langle r,\alpha^\vee\rangle>0$. The other coefficient of $s_\alpha r$ is still positive, hence its two coefficients are nonnegative by the base axiom. Its height is smaller by the positive integer $\langle r,\alpha^\vee\rangle$. Induction ends at a simple root; negatives lie in the same orbits since $s_\alpha\alpha=-\alpha$. For the orthogonal case the reflections are $(i,j)\mapsto(-i,j),(i,-j)$. In the other cases they are $U(i,j)=(-i+mj,j)$ and $T(i,j)=(i,i-j)$. Direct substitution shows that the union of each displayed positive list in the statement and its negative is stable under both maps. Conversely $c=T(a)$, $d=U(b)$ in $B_2$; in $G_2$, $c=T(a)$, $d=U(c)$, $e=U(b)$, $f=T(e)$. These generate every displayed positive vector, and the negatives follow by reflecting a simple root before applying the same word. The orbit computation proves exactly the four lists for the original base.

source.place: Step 2, printed pp.205--206; explicit height induction and four finite reflection computations.

proof.text: Conjugation by $n_\alpha$ identifies the root modules of $r$ and $s_\alpha r$, since differentiating an invertible conjugation gives an invertible linear map and carries the torus character to its reflected character. The reflection formulas of step 2 therefore show that all displayed $X_r$ are generators of the indicated modules; a sign does not change this. Apply the integral positive-adjoint model. In $A_2$ its $(a,b)$ string has $q=1$, $V_0=X_b$, and $V_1=[X_a,X_b]=-X_c$, so $\operatorname{Ad}(n_a)X_b=-X_c$. In $B_2$ the string has $q=2$ and $V_1=-X_c$; its Weyl formula is $\operatorname{Ad}(n_a)V_1=-V_1$, which gives $\operatorname{Ad}(n_a)X_c=-X_c$. No cancellation by $2$ was used.

source.place: Step 2 and Lemma 6.2.8, printed pp.205--208; the string signs are extracted from the separately stated linear-action input.

proof.text:
For a listed pair $(r,s)$ let $\Psi=\Phi\cap(\mathbf Z_{\geq0}r+\mathbf Z_{\geq0}s)$. It is closed under root sums and contains no opposite roots. The root-product theorem gives $H=U_\Psi$, with coordinates $x_t(z_t)=\exp_t(z_tX_t)$ in any order. Put $F=x_s(y)x_r(x)$ and let $F'$ be the proposed right side, with the following explicit correction factors in order:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|l}A_2&(a,b)&c(xy)\\ B_2&(a,b)&c(xy),d(x^2y)\\ B_2&(a,c)&d(2xy)\\ G_2&(a,b)&c(xy),d(x^2y),e(x^3y),f(x^3y^2)\\ G_2&(a,c)&d(2xy),f(3xy^2),e(3x^2y)\\ G_2&(a,d)&e(3xy)\\ G_2&(b,e)&f(-xy).\end{array}$$
Here $t(z)$ abbreviates $x_t(z)$, and $F'$ starts with $x_r(x)x_s(y)$. Each row is in increasing $(i+j,i)$ for its pair; in particular the $(a,c)$ row puts $f$ before $e$. Each expression is a morphism into $H$, sends $(0,0)$ to $1$, and is $T$-equivariant for input characters $(r,s)$: a factor $x_{ir+js}(Kx^iy^j)$ transforms by exactly $ir+js$.

source.place: Step 3 and Example 6.2.9, printed pp.207--209; explicit candidates, with the product order specified in the item.

proof.text:
Use right logarithmic derivatives in the dual-number sense of the rigidity lemma. Multiplying $u(x+\epsilon)$ by $v(x+\epsilon)$ and then by $(uv)(x)^{-1}$ gives
$$\delta_t(uv)=\delta_tu+\operatorname{Ad}(u)\delta_tv.$$
Indeed write $u(t+\epsilon)=(1+\epsilon\delta_tu)u(t)$ and similarly for $v$; multiply and discard $\epsilon^2$. For $u=x_r(h(x,y))$, the homomorphism property and the differential normalization of the root exponential give $\delta_tu=X_r\partial_t h$. Thus for a word $x_{r_1}(h_1)\cdots x_{r_l}(h_l)$ one successively adds
$$P_{r_1}(h_1)\cdots P_{r_{k-1}}(h_{k-1})X_{r_k}\,\partial_t h_k.$$
The matrices are the integer polynomials of the adjoint model; all inputs here lie in the positive tangent modules. These equations reduce the comparison to finite polynomial addition and multiplication over $\mathbf Z[x,y]$.

source.place: Auxiliary dual-number calculation in the coordinate setting of Step 3, printed p.207; written by Q90.

proof.text:
For $A_2$, $P_a(z)X_b=X_b-zX_c$ and $P_b(z)X_a=X_a+zX_c$. Applying step 5 to $F'$ with $c(xy)$ gives $\delta_xF'=X_a+yX_c$ and $\delta_yF'=X_b$: the $-xX_c$ from $x_b(y)$ cancels $xX_c$ from the last factor. These equal the derivatives of $F$. For $B_2$ use
$$P_a(z)X_b=X_b-zX_c+z^2X_d,\quad P_a(z)X_c=X_c-2zX_d,\quad P_b(z)X_a=X_a+zX_c,\quad P_c(z)X_a=X_a+2zX_d.$$
For $(a,b)$ the successive extra contributions to $\delta_xF'$ are $y(X_c-2xX_d)$ and $2xyX_d$, giving $X_a+yX_c$. For $\delta_yF'$ they are $x(X_c-2xX_d)$ and $x^2X_d$, which cancel the correction in $P_a(x)X_b$ and give $X_b$. For $(a,c)$ the single factor $d(2xy)$ gives $\delta_xF'=X_a+2yX_d$ and $\delta_yF'=X_c$. These are $\operatorname{Ad}(x_s(y))X_r$ and $X_s$, respectively, as required.

source.place: Step 3 and Lemma 6.2.8, printed pp.207--208; explicit A2 and B2 polynomial checks.

proof.text:
For $G_2$ the nonidentity positive-basis columns of the adjoint matrices are
$$\begin{aligned}P_a(z)X_b&=X_b-zX_c+z^2X_d-z^3X_e,&P_a(z)X_c&=X_c-2zX_d+3z^2X_e,&P_a(z)X_d&=X_d-3zX_e,\\ P_b(z)X_a&=X_a+zX_c,&P_b(z)X_e&=X_e+zX_f,\\ P_c(z)X_a&=X_a+2zX_d-3z^2X_f,&P_c(z)X_d&=X_d-3zX_f,\\ P_d(z)X_a&=X_a+3zX_e,&P_d(z)X_c&=X_c+3zX_f,&P_e(z)X_b&=X_b-zX_f.\end{aligned}$$
All unlisted columns are unchanged. For $(a,b)$, the $c,d,e,f$ factors contribute to $\delta_xF'$ respectively
$$y(X_c-2xX_d+3x^2X_e),\quad 2xy(X_d-3xX_e-3xyX_f),\quad3x^2y(X_e+yX_f),\quad3x^2y^2X_f.$$
Together with the first $X_a$ these sum to $X_a+yX_c$. Their contributions to $\delta_yF'$ are the same columns multiplied respectively by $x,x^2,x^3,2x^3y$ instead of $y,2xy,3x^2y,3x^2y^2$. Adding $P_a(x)X_b$ gives $X_b$. Hence both derivatives agree with those of $F$.

source.place: Example 6.2.9, printed pp.208--209, with the omitted (a,b) multiplication expanded using the separate linear-action input.

proof.text:
Continue with the same $G_2$ columns. For $(a,c)$ the proposed factor order is $d(2xy),f(3xy^2),e(3x^2y)$. Their contributions to $\delta_xF'$ are
$$2y(X_d-3xX_e-3yX_f),\quad3y^2X_f,\quad6xyX_e,$$
so $\delta_xF'=X_a+2yX_d-3y^2X_f$. Their contributions to $\delta_yF'$ are $2x(X_d-3xX_e-3yX_f),6xyX_f,3x^2X_e$; adding $P_a(x)X_c$ gives $X_c$. For $(a,d)$ the single factor $e(3xy)$ yields $\delta_xF'=X_a+3yX_e$ and $\delta_yF'=X_d$. For $(b,e)$ the single factor $f(-xy)$ yields $\delta_xF'=X_b-yX_f$ and $\delta_yF'=X_e$. In each case these are precisely $P_s(y)X_r$ and $X_s$, the two derivatives of $F$. Thus all seven comparisons hold as polynomial identities over the integers.

source.place: Example 6.2.9, equations (6.2.9), printed pp.208--209; same finite matrix calculation for the item product order.

proof.text: Apply primitive-weight logarithmic rigidity to each comparison in $H=U_\Psi$. In the coordinates relative to $(r,s)$ the possible weights are the axes $(1,0),(0,1)$ and: for $(a,b)$, $(1,1)$ and where present $(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)$; for $(a,c)$ in $B_2$, $(1,1)$; for $(a,c)$ in $G_2$, $(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)$; for $(a,d)$ and $(b,e)$, just $(1,1)$. Every pair has gcd $1$, so the lemma applies even over rings of characteristic $2$ or $3$ or with nilpotents. Steps 6--8 give its two derivative hypotheses, and step 4 gives its morphism and equivariance hypotheses. Hence $F=F'$ as morphisms. The integer parameters in step 4 are fixed by the type and the specified normalization, so they give the required simultaneous constants for every lattice and realization. The canonical exponentials, conjugations and coordinate products commute with base change, and evaluation of integer polynomials commutes with every ring map. Thus all the asserted identities hold on every algebra and after arbitrary base change. In type $A_1\times A_1$ the only positive roots are $a,b$ and there are no listed pairs or tangent identities to prove.
